criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community on-site sanitation service access (lined pit latrine construction, formal pit-emptying / scheduled desludging services, and water supply needed for toilet functionality) in George Compound, a peri-urban settlement in Lusaka, Zambia.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines legal, regulatory, institutional, and governance arrangements for peri-urban on-site sanitation involving NWASCO, ZEMA, Lusaka City Council (LCC), LWSC, and D-WASH structures. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, although several themes cover generic behavioural sensitization and physical infrastructure (FSTPs, roads, pit depth), the empirical findings also directly examine specific rule-type mechanisms governing service access: (1) regulatory/institutional expansion of LWSC's formal mandate from water and sewerage only to include peri-urban on-site sanitation; (2) tariff, cost-recovery, and payment rules, including mandatory pit-latrine registration and small routine fee contributions for scheduled desludging, initial tariff subsidies to keep desludging charges affordable, lack of instalment payment options for toilet construction excluding capital-constrained households, and utility billing despite non-supply of water; and (3) Public Health Act enforcement inspections, litigation threats compelling sanitation compliance/connection, service-provider licensing/registration with LWSC and ZEMA, and gaps in statutory instruments for minimum latrine standards.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary qualitative empirical evidence from an interpretive phenomenological study using in-depth interviews and key informant interviews with 29 participants in George Compound and relevant Lusaka sanitation institutions, analysed via Braun and Clarke's six-step reflexive thematic analysis. Per review safeguards, qualitative empirical studies of rule-type mechanisms are eligible for systematic review inclusion.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative outcomes relevant to sanitation service availability, predictability, affordability, household access, and exclusion, including improved predictability and affordability of pit emptying under registered scheduled desludging and subsidies, formal service availability following LWSC's mandate expansion, financial exclusion from toilet construction where upfront rather than instalment payment is required (leaving women reliant on shared or unavailable toilets), and billing without reliable water supply.
criterion_notes.c5: Population, unit of analysis (beneficiary households/residents and institutional stakeholders assessing household-level peri-urban sanitation in George Compound, Lusaka; N = 29), rule-type exposures, qualitative access/affordability outcomes, and study design (interpretive phenomenological qualitative study) are all identifiable from the full text.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English (interviews conducted in English or translated from local languages by the researcher).

evidence_quotes.quote: “A customer in the peri-urban area must register that they have a pit latrine; once they register, they paid a small amount towards desludging. So that when the toilet fills up, they just call the service provider.”
The mandate of LWSC expanded from focusing solely on water supply and sewerage system to also covering sanitation service delivery. This institutional shift closed a long-standing service gap.

the public health Act compels households and provides guidance and failure to comply with them might to courts litigations. Hence the law compels the people to have sanitation facilities, hence this helps in improving household sanitation.
Therefore, the researcher determined sample size after conducting interviews with 29 Participants (10 Males and 15 women) and 4 key informants.
"LWSC needs to seriously consider supplying water in the area because despite not supplying water, they bill us. Most of our money is spent on buying water for household use."

The study revealed that the introduction of scheduled desludging has improved predictability and affordability in pit emptying services. Under this system, households register their pit latrines and make small, routine contributions, which enables service providers to plan operations efficiently and reduces the risk of full pits overflowing or being emptied unsafely.

raw_response.exposure: Legal, regulatory, institutional, and tariff/payment mechanisms governing peri-urban on-site sanitation: expansion of LWSC's utility mandate to cover on-site sanitation, mandatory pit-latrine registration and routine contribution fee rules for scheduled desludging, initial service subsidies, upfront vs. instalment payment structures for toilet construction, utility water billing rules, Public Health Act enforcement inspections, and ZEMA/NWASCO licensing and statutory minimum standards.
raw_response.outcome: Qualitative household sanitation access, pit-emptying service availability and predictability, affordability of desludging and toilet construction, compliance, and gendered barriers to toilet and water access in a peri-urban informal settlement.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Sanitation programme beneficiaries and institutional stakeholders (Ward Development Committee, Water and Sanitation Committee, Lusaka City Council Public Health Department, ZEMA Inspectorate, NWASCO, and LWSC Peri-Urban Department) in George Compound, Lusaka, Zambia; purposive sample of 29 participants (25 community beneficiaries: 10 men and 15 women; plus 4 key informants).
raw_response.rationale: Full-text qualitative empirical study (interpretive phenomenology with reflexive thematic analysis of 29 interviews) examining peri-urban household on-site sanitation and pit-emptying access in George Compound, Lusaka, Zambia. Although framed broadly around stakeholder-perceived mitigation measures (including education and physical infrastructure), the primary empirical findings directly examine multiple rule-type mechanisms under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope — including expansion of the commercial utility's regulatory mandate to cover peri-urban on-site sanitation, pit-latrine registration and routine contribution tariff/subsidy rules for scheduled desludging, upfront vs. instalment payment barriers to toilet construction, billing without water delivery, and Public Health Act enforcement and provider licensing — alongside qualitative outcomes on service availability, predictability, affordability, and exclusion. Eligible for inclusion in the systematic review's qualitative mechanism synthesis (medium confidence given the broad exploratory framing alongside concrete mechanism evidence).
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative interpretive phenomenological study (in-depth interviews and key informant interviews analysed with reflexive thematic analysis)
